Amir hadi@AmirHadiEng · Nov 8

A Tesla Optimus engineer showed GROXIE, a compact physical AI assistant for a kitchen counter or desk, a side project inspired by his wife (1,406 likes).

Excited to share a small project I've been leading alongside our larger robotics work at @Tesla_Optimus, and one I'm particularly excited about.

The inspiration actually came from my wife. We started exploring the idea of a compact physical AI assistant that could sit on a kitchen counter or desk and help with everyday tasks.

During our development, she began testing GROXIE at home while cooking, using it to suggest meals based on available ingredients, walk her through recipes, manage her calendar, draft emails, make calls, and provide real-time updates throughout the day.

What makes GROXIE interesting is the idea of integrating @grok AI as its conversational intelligence.

Using @grok would power GROXIE's ability to understand natural conversations, answer complex questions, provide information, and adapt to individual preferences. Combined with expressive robotic movements, voice recognition, and a personalized assistant interface, the goal is to make AI feel more natural and accessible.

Rather than building another full-sized humanoid robot, we wanted to explore how much useful intelligence could fit into a compact desktop companion.

The next step in this concept is a formal prototype review, where we'd evaluate the hardware, AI integration, privacy, safety, and reliability before considering approval for further development or a potential consumer release.

I'm excited about where this could go.

MrNetwork@encrypt_wizard · Nov 8

Joust, an entry for the Nous Research Hermes Agent plugin hackathon: three AI agents race to fix the same bug, each in its own Git worktree (65 likes).

Introducing Joust, my entry for the Hermes Agent Plugin Hackathon @NousResearch

Ask three AI agents to fix the same bug in one folder and they overwrite each other.

Joust gives every contender its own Git worktree and its own Hermes subagent, and it can run each one on a different model.

In the demo, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro raced to fix a real order-book bug.

All three passed the official tests, three runs each, in under two and a half minutes.

Then Crossfire fired each model's own tests at its rivals.

Gemini had outscored GPT on points, but both rivals caught it dropping leftover quantity on partial fills, a bug the official suite never tested. Gemini fell to last.

Claude won with 91.5 points, and its fix ran in 3.65 ms against 260 ms for the old code.

The winner merges only after you approve it in Hermes's own approval card.

Every attempt is kept as a Git branch, and one call rolls the merge back.

Real run, nothing mocked.

Built on Hermes hooks, middleware and the subagent lifecycle, with a full arena inside Hermes Desktop.

May the best patch win.

An optimistic AI future view drawn from “Rise and Fall of American Growth”: 1870 to 1920 solved plumbing, electrification and more (315 likes).

Ethan Mollick@emollick
A favorite optimistic view of the future of AI is from a pessimistic book that not about AI: "Rise and Fall of American Growth," which argues that we had a one-time explosion in living standards from 1870 and 1920 (& later outside the US).

In 1870: no toilets, no city plumbing, lamp light, no central heating, little public health, horses for local travel, etc. In 50 years, all of this was solved & the nation was electrified. In the next fifty modern medicine, air travel and telecommunication happened.

The book then points out that we have had no changes in lifestyle of similar scale since the 1970s. Written in 2016, it argued that we would likely never experience another boom like the "Special Century." The positive view of AI should make us ask "But what if we do?" and "How do we make it all go right?"
